title: A mother-in-law and a whole town (Mark 1:29–39)
hookLine: he heals Peter's mother-in-law, the whole town crowds the door, and before dawn he slips off to pray

cards: Same Sabbath, a few hours later. They walk out of the synagogue, still buzzing, and go straight to Simon and Andrew's house for a meal. Yes, Simon, the one known as Peter, had a house, a wife, and a mother-in-law.
And she's in bed with a fever. A crowded little house, a sick relative, guests arriving, nobody cooking. By sundown, the whole town will be at that door.
And the next morning, before anyone is awake, Jesus will be gone.

teach.h: HE TOOK HER BY THE HAND.
teach.b: Mark tells it in three scenes. Scene one, the bedroom. They tell Jesus about her right away.
In the King James Bible: "And he came and took her by the hand, and lifted her up; and immediately the fever left her, and she ministered unto them."
He takes her hand and lifts her up, and that word, raised, is the same word later used for resurrection. Then she serves them. Some readers wince, as if she's healed just to make lunch.

But the word is diakoneō, the root of deacon, and it's the very word Mark uses for what Jesus came to do: not to be served, but to serve. In Mark, only the angels in the desert have done it before her. Scene two, sundown.
The Sabbath ends when the sun sets, which may be why they wait: now they can carry their sick.

teach.h: ALL THE CITY AT THE DOOR.
teach.b: "And all the city was gathered together at the door." The whole town, in the dusk, at one little doorway. He heals many.

"And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed." Mark piles up three Greek words for it: very early, still night, extremely.
His friends, Simon leading, hunt him down: "All men seek for thee."

teach.h: LET US GO INTO THE NEXT TOWNS.
teach.b: And Jesus answers: "Let us go into the next towns, that I may preach there also: for therefore came I forth."
He doesn't stay to become Capernaum's celebrity healer. The prayer in the dark seems to have told him where to go next. Luke showed this rhythm back in the sabbath days: he withdrew.
Mark shows it on day one.

how: Many Christians rise early to pray, following Jesus's example in Mark 1:35, and monastic communities keep prayers in the dark before dawn, often called vigils or matins.

o: to serve, the root of the word deacon
to lift up someone who is sick
to pray alone before the sun comes up

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.
p: the Sabbath ends; the town arrives

s: the gospels show that Peter was married
he had a mother-in-law, and Paul also mentions Peter's wife.
the crowd came at sundown by chance
Mark marks the moment: when the sun set, the Sabbath ended, and the sick could be carried to the door.
Jesus stayed in Capernaum because everyone was looking for him
he said: let us go into the next towns, that I may preach there also.

games.q: you're Jesus. the whole town was at the door last night, and this morning everyone is looking for you. Simon finds you praying. what do you do?
o: go back and keep healing in Capernaum.
move on to the next towns to preach there too.
stay hidden in the solitary place.
games.why: "let us go into the next towns, that I may preach there also: for therefore came I forth." the prayer in the dark pointed him onward.

practice: Picture tomorrow morning, ten minutes earlier than usual, while the house is still dark and quiet, before the town is at your door: a chair, a window, the edge of the bed.
If you pray, picture praying there; if you don't, picture simply sitting and listening to the quiet. You don't need to decide anything big; just let those ten minutes become real in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Diakoneō, the word for serve, used of Simon's mother-in-law after her fever left her, and of why Jesus said he came at all.

orig.note: Greek: early, in the night, very — Mark's triple way of saying a great while before day (1:35).

carryVoice: Your line: a great while before day. Before the crowd, he found the quiet. Day one hundred sixty-one, done.
